key_risks.description: Expense growth is running ahead of the guide. Q2 total noninterest expense was $27.3 billion, up 15%, on revenue-related compensation, wage inflation, headcount growth, brokerage and distribution fees, marketing, technology and occupancy. The roughly $107.5 billion adjusted expense guide implies H2 expense below the Q2 pace. That is hard to reconcile with revenue-linked pay if fees stay strong, and the adjusted-to-reported bridge is not shown in the excerpts.

Credit support may be thin. The Q2 provision of $2.5 billion (down from $2.8 billion) was supported by net charge-offs of $2.4 billion, down only $44 million. The net reserve build was $149 million, primarily in Wholesale, and Q1 included a $128 million consumer release tied to home prices. Adverse-scenario sensitivities of about $4.8 billion for credit card and $5.0 billion for wholesale show a modest cushion against a macro shock.

Net interest income depends on volatile Markets activity. Markets NII was $1.9 billion in Q2 vs $0.56 billion a year earlier, while NII excluding Markets grew only 4% to $23.7 billion. The ex-Markets net yield slipped to 3.65% from 3.71%. The full-year guide is explicitly market dependent and implies a sequential H2 step-up.

Balance sheet growth is concentrated in Markets and securities financing. Trading assets rose 32% to $1.06 trillion, securities borrowed rose 27%, and repurchase funding rose to $704.9 billion from $442.4 billion. Long-term debt rose to $460.5 billion on net structured note issuance in Markets. This raises sensitivity to client activity, funding conditions and risk-weighted asset (RWA) growth.

key_risks.description: Regulatory capital requirements may rise. The Standardized CET1 requirement, including buffers, was 11.5% against a 14.2% actual ratio, which has fallen from 15.1% a year earlier. The Firm expects the U.S. Basel III and GSIB surcharge re-proposals, taken together, to raise required CET1 capital by about 4%, which could limit buyback expansion.

Earnings quality is affected by non-recurring items. Q2 noninterest revenue includes a $4.6 billion net gain related to Visa shares, and Investment Banking revenue includes net gains on equity investments. The effective tax rate rose to about 23% in Q2 from about 18% a year earlier, when Corporate included a $774 million tax benefit, so year-over-year comparisons are flattered.

Rate sensitivity remains a headwind if rates fall. The earnings-at-risk disclosure shows a -200bp parallel shift costing about $5.1 billion, versus $6.0 billion at year-end. The narrower exposure is positive, but the guide still depends on lower rates not compressing deposit and loan margins faster than balance growth offsets.

The Apple Card forward purchase commitment adds consumer credit exposure. The transaction is expected to close about 24 months after the December 30, 2025 commitment and will add to card balances and charge-off exposure.

bull_case: Q2 2026 net income was $21.2 billion, up about 41%, with diluted EPS of $7.70 vs $5.24. Six-month ROE reached 22% vs 18% and the overhead ratio improved to 51% from 53%.

Capital generation comfortably funds the payout. Six-month net income applicable to common equity of $37.1 billion covered $8.1 billion of dividends and $13.8 billion of net treasury stock purchases, and CET1 capital still grew about $14.2 billion to $302.6 billion. A new $50 billion repurchase authorization became effective July 1, 2026 and the quarterly dividend was lifted to $1.65.

Fee franchises are compounding. Investment Banking revenue was $3.9 billion, up 45%, with fees up 30%, and the Firm ranked #2 globally. Asset Management revenue was $3.3 billion, up 23%, on higher average market levels and strong net inflows.

Core spread income is growing on volume. NII excluding Markets was $23.7 billion, up 4%, on higher deposits, revolving card balances and wholesale loans despite lower rates. Management raised full-year NII guidance to about $105.5 billion.
Card Services & Auto revenue grew 12% and the Apple Card portfolio adds a long-dated growth option. The deposit-token and Kinexys stack could widen the deposit moat over time.
The balance sheet has ample cushion. The CET1 ratio of 14.2% compares with a requirement of 11.5%, and the allowance for credit losses of $31.5 billion (1.79% of retained loans) remains substantial.
bear_case: Headline growth is flattered by non-recurring items: a $4.6 billion Visa share gain, net gains on equity investments in Investment Banking, and a lower year-over-year effective tax rate comparison. Run-rate earnings power is lower than the reported $7.70 diluted EPS suggests.

The NII guide is market dependent. Markets NII was $1.9 billion in Q2, ex-Markets growth was only 4%, and the ex-Markets net yield slipped to 3.65% from 3.71%. The $105.5 billion guide implies roughly $27.3 billion of NII per quarter in H2 vs $25.5 billion reported in Q2 (about +7%), a ramp that depends on volatile trading balances.

Expense growth of 15% in Q2 is hard to square with the roughly $107.5 billion adjusted expense guide, which implies about $26.7 billion per quarter in H2 vs $27.3 billion in Q2 if the definitions are comparable. Revenue-linked compensation should not fall if fees stay strong, so operating leverage is not assured.

Credit support is thin. Net charge-offs fell only $44 million, the net reserve build was $149 million and the allowance is flat year to date. Adverse-scenario sensitivities of about $4.8 billion for card and $5.0 billion for wholesale could reverse provision relief quickly.

The CET1 ratio has declined for four consecutive quarters, to 14.2% from 15.1%, because RWA growth is outpacing capital. Basel III and GSIB re-proposals could raise required CET1 by about 4%, which supports holding the buyback pace flat rather than expanding it.

Balance sheet growth in trading assets (+32%) and repo financing is client-activity dependent and consumes capital. Unverified secondary reports of a sharply lower buyback pace add noise until management confirms the repurchase run rate.

what_to_watch.text:
**Net Interest Income Guide and the H2 Ramp:** Management guides to about $105.5 billion of full-year NII and $96.5 billion ex-Markets, up from $103 billion previously. H1 NII was $50.9 billion, so the guide implies roughly $27.3 billion per quarter in H2 vs $25.5 billion in Q2, and the implied $9 billion of Markets NII needs about $4.9 billion in H2 vs $4.1 billion in H1. NII ex-Markets grew 4% on deposit, card revolving and wholesale loan growth, which is a volume-driven base. However, the ex-Markets net yield compressed to 3.65% from 3.71% and the guide is explicitly market dependent, so the raise depends on trading activity holding up. Later news cites a further raise to about $106.2 billion, which must be reconciled to company disclosure.

-> Monitor Markets NII, NII ex-Markets vs the roughly $24 billion-plus quarterly run rate needed, the ex-Markets net yield, and any revision to the $105.5 billion and $96.5 billion guides.

**Fee Momentum and the Beat-and-Raise Setup:** Investment Banking revenue was $3.9 billion, up 45%, with fees up 30% and a #2 global ranking. Management has already raised NII guidance, and Asset Management revenue grew 23%, which supports an upside setup. However, the Investment Banking gain includes net gains on equity investments that are not durable. The NII guide already requires about a 7% sequential step-up with ex-Markets growth of only 4%, so a beat is not assured and a miss is plausible. Post-period news also shows Investment Banking fees falling 8% sequentially despite year-over-year growth.

-> Monitor Investment Banking fee trends and pipeline commentary, equity investment gains vs fees, and Asset Management net inflows against the guide.

**Capital Returns and CET1:** H1 net income applicable to common equity of $37.1 billion covered $8.1 billion of dividends and $13.8 billion of net treasury stock purchases, and CET1 capital grew about $14.2 billion to $302.6 billion. Repurchases were $6.7 billion in Q2 and $15.0 billion in H1, in line with a year earlier, and a new $50 billion authorization began July 1 with about $18.4 billion left under the prior program. However, the CET1 ratio has slid to 14.2% from 15.1% on RWA growth, and the Basel III and GSIB re-proposals could raise required CET1 by about 4%. Secondary reports of a sharp buyback cut cite figures that conflict with the filed data and remain unconfirmed.

-> Monitor quarterly gross repurchases vs the roughly $7.5 billion H1 run rate, the CET1 ratio vs the 11.5% requirement, and any commentary on the pace under the new $50 billion authorization.

**Expense Trajectory and Operating Leverage:** Q2 noninterest expense was $27.3 billion, up 15%, driven by revenue-related compensation, wage inflation and headcount growth. Annualized, that is about $109 billion against a roughly $107.5 billion adjusted expense guide, implying H2 spending near $26.7 billion per quarter. Fee strength in wealth and investment banking means variable compensation should scale with revenue, and the adjusted and reported definitions may differ. However, if revenue cools the fee thesis weakens, and if it does not, expenses may overshoot, so margin expansion is not guaranteed. Later news cites an expense forecast raised to about $108.6 billion.

-> Monitor adjusted expense vs the guide, the adjusted-to-reported bridge, the overhead ratio and compensation commentary.

**Credit Quality and Reserve Posture:** The Q2 provision was $2.5 billion vs $2.8 billion, net charge-offs were $2.4 billion (down $44 million), and the allowance coverage ratio was 1.79% vs 1.85%. Management lowered the full-year Card Services net charge-off rate guidance to about 3.2% from 3.4%, which supports a benign view. However, the net reserve build of $149 million was concentrated in Wholesale and the allowance is flat year to date, so lower provisions reflect smaller builds more than demonstrated improvement. Adverse-scenario sensitivities of roughly $4.8 billion for card and $5.0 billion for wholesale show how fast the benefit could reverse.

-> Monitor the Card Services net charge-off rate vs the guide, the size and mix of the net reserve build, wholesale nonaccruals and the allowance coverage ratio.

**Card Franchise and the Apple Card Transaction:** Card Services & Auto revenue rose 12% to $7.76 billion in Q2 and 13% in H1, supporting the case that card economics cushion rate sensitivity alongside deposit growth. The Apple Card forward purchase commitment is expected to close about 24 months after December 30, 2025, so it is optionality rather than near-term earnings. However, card NII depends on revolving balances and card is also the main source of net charge-offs, so the diversification away from rates comes with greater credit-cycle exposure. Auto operating lease income of $1.2 billion also contributed to growth.

-> Monitor card loan and revolving balance growth, Card NII, the card charge-off rate and any update on Apple Card closing timing and portfolio size.

**Markets Balance Sheet Growth and Funding:** Trading assets rose 32% to $1.06 trillion, securities borrowed rose 27%, and repurchase funding rose to $704.9 billion from $442.4 billion. Long-term debt reached $460.5 billion on net structured note issuance tied to client demand, and the filing links this growth to client-driven activity and prime brokerage. This supports Markets revenue and NII, but it also drives RWA growth and the decline in the CET1 ratio. On the other hand, a larger financing book carries more sensitivity to market conditions.

-> Monitor trading assets, RWA growth, structured note issuance and Markets NII and noninterest revenue together.

**Deposit Franchise, Tokenized Deposits and AI Agents:** Deposits rose to $2.71 trillion from $2.56 trillion, driven in part by net inflows in Corporate and Investment Bank Payments. Kinexys and JPM Coin extend the deposit franchise toward on-chain settlement, and management has said it blocks outside AI agents that log in with customer credentials. However, the filing gives no Kinexys revenue or deposit-token volume, so this is a strategic option rather than a sized earnings driver.

-> Monitor deposit growth and mix, Payments volumes and any quantified disclosure on tokenized deposits or agentic-payments policy.

hypotheses_explored.question: Is JPM's NII growth of 10% in Q2 2026 broad-based, or is it being driven by Markets NII that may not repeat?
hypotheses_explored.summary: The 10% reported NII growth in Q2 is largely a Markets story: Markets NII rose to $1.9B from $0.56B while NII excluding Markets grew only 4% to $23.7B. The ex-Markets net yield compressed to 3.65% from 3.71% and the managed net yield fell to 2.40% from 2.43%. Core spread income is growing on balance-sheet volume and not on margin, so the guidance raise to $105.5B is sensitive to trading activity. A counterpoint is that Markets NII is largely offset by Markets noninterest revenue and the ex-Markets guide is the cleaner signal.
evidence_quotes: Net interest income excluding Markets was $23.7 billion, up 4%, driven by higher deposit balances, higher revolving balances in Card Services and higher wholesale loan balances, largely offset by the impact of lower rates.

hypotheses_explored.question: Can JPM's fee momentum and NII ex-Markets outlook support upside to the full-year 2026 guidance, given Investment Banking strength and the recent guidance raise?
hypotheses_explored.summary: Investment Banking is re-accelerating with share gains, and management has lifted NII ex-Markets guidance and set a preliminary 2027 estimate, which points to a possible beat-and-raise setup. However, the guidance is explicitly market dependent, the Investment Banking gain includes non-durable equity investment gains, and the guide already requires about a 7% sequential NII step-up with ex-Markets growth of only 4%. News NII figures for Q3 do not reconcile with the filing's Q2 NII of $25.5B and should be checked against official releases.
evidence_quotes: Investment Banking revenue was $3.9 billion, up 45%, predominantly driven by higher investment banking fees and net gains on equity investments. Investment banking fees were up 30%, driven by higher fees across all products, with particularly strong performance in equity underwriting fees.
The Firm ranked #2 for global investment banking fees for the three months ended June 30, 2026, according to Dealogic.
Management expects net interest income to be approximately $105.5 billion and net interest income excluding Markets to be approximately $96.5 billion, market dependent.
The bank raised its full-year net interest income forecast to about $106.2 billion, up from $105.5 billion.
The bank also raised its full-year outlook for net interest income excluding Markets and provided a preliminary estimate of approximately $107 billion for 2027.
